newsitem.title: USA: US air safety board seeks Boeing 737 safety changes.
newsitem.headline: US air safety board seeks Boeing 737 safety changes.

text.p: U.S. safety officials on Wednesday recommended immediate sweeping changes in the rudder and yaw control systems of the widely-used Boeing Co 737 to try to avoid sudden and uncontrolled rolls.

Included in the National Transportation Safety Board's recommendations to the Federal Aviation Administration were rudder design changes by Boeing and new training for pilots on how to combat such uncommanded movements.

The board's recommendations followed a series of still-unexplained crashes by 737s, including USAir Group Inc flight 427 near Pittsburgh on September 8, 1994, which killed all 132 people on board. While causes of the incidents have not been determined, investigators believe they were triggered by sharp sudden rolls before coming in for landings.
Officials said the changes might not get to the cause of the accidents but would generally make 737s safer.
The FAA last August, after its own review of the 737, proposed a series of changes to improve the safety of what it called a safe aircraft.
Some 2,600 737s are flown by airlines worldwide.

The board recommended the FAA require Boeing to make long-term design changes to preclude a loss of control from a rudder "hard-over" -- an extreme rudder shift that could throw the plane into a sharp roll.

It also recommended a redesign as needed of the plane's rudder damper system to prevent yaw -- the movement of the nose from side to side -- so the rudder would not move into an extreme roll-causing position. In addition, the board called for an indicator system to show the pilot the position and movement of the rudder, an indicator not now in the cockpit.
The board also stressed the need to develop additional training procedures by Boeing and 737 operators to require crews to disengage the yaw damper in case of an uncontrolled roll.

It added that Boeing should develop procedures for 737 pilots to effectively deal with a sudden uncommanded rudder movement and 737 operators to give the necessary training to pilots on how to get out ot an uncontrolled roll.
The FAA and Boeing had no immediate comment on the board's recommendations.
